How the ratings work

The short version of a 50-page methodology.

1. Pressure = leverage, not the clock

A win-probability model for both innings (tested on unseen 2025-26 matches: Brier 0.164 vs 0.176 for a logistic baseline) gives every ball a Dynamic Pressure Index: the expected swing in win probability the ball can cause. DPI 1 is an average ball. The top 20% (DPI ≥ 1.27) are pressure balls. Tested against match results, a run above expectation on those balls is worth 2.4× an ordinary run; on "death overs" it is worth 0.91×, on "RRR ≥ 10" 0.78×.

2. Performance = runs above expectation (RAE)

Every ball is compared with what an average player would do in exactly the same situation (balls left, wickets, required rate, batting position, competition, season). Wickets are converted into runs using a Duckworth-Lewis-style resource curve fitted to this data, so one number captures scoring and survival (or runs saved and wickets taken).

3. Fair comparison = the Pressure-Adjusted Player Model

A random-effects model estimates each player's normal level, pressure level and shift, while adjusting for the opponent on every ball. Runs and dismissals are shrunk separately by cross-validation: scoring under pressure turned out to be the same skill as scoring generally, while dismissal risk under pressure genuinely varies between players.

4. Uncertainty = 500 match bootstraps

The Clutch Rating is the 20th percentile of each player's bootstrap distribution: we are 80% confident he is at least this good under pressure. It rewards a long, repeatable record over a short hot streak. P(top 10) is the share of resamples in which he stays top ten.

5. Eligibility and safeguards

Batters need 120+ pressure balls and bowlers 180+, across 10+ matches and 2+ seasons. Ratings within 1 run are ordered by how often the player stays top ten across 18 core robustness specifications. A player is only selected if his observed pressure record is above expectation (the "evidence gate").

About the filters

Filtered numbers are descriptive, computed from the same ball-level expectations. Small slices are noisy, so watch the sample badges. The final rankings deliberately do not move with filters.
